summary: Describes the LISP mapping service built from Map-Resolvers and Map-Servers, which give a simple front end to databases mapping endpoint identifiers to routing locators. It was replaced by RFC 9301.

eli5.summary: A front desk where you ask where does this person live now, and the desk checks the big address books for you.

subtitle: A simplified interface for looking up where network addresses are located

tldr.problem: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) separates the address space into two parts, but routers need a simple way to find the mapping between a device's ID and its location on the network without dealing with complex database systems.
tldr.mechanism: Map-Servers and Map-Resolvers act as intermediaries: Map-Servers register the ID-to-location mappings from routers, and Map-Resolvers answer lookups from routers without requiring them to connect to a complex mapping database.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now use a simple registration and query interface instead of implementing complex database protocols, making LISP deployment simpler and cheaper. RFC 9301 updated this specification.

facts.label: Quick registration period
facts.value: five minutes, up to every 20 seconds

facts.label: Negative Map-Reply TTL
facts.value: 15 minutes (15 minutes for non-existent EIDs, 1 minute for registered gaps)

today: RFC 6833 is an Experimental specification. It was obsoleted by RFC 9301, which updates the LISP mapping service definition.

sections.title: Introduction to LISP Mapping
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) divides the Internet address space in two: Endpoint IDs (EIDs) identify devices within a site, and Routing Locators (RLOCs) are the device's actual location on the Internet backbone. To make this work, the network needs a database that maps each EID to the RLOC of the router that can reach it. This RFC defines two new device types that simplify managing this mapping database: the Map-Resolver and the Map-Server.

These devices are modeled loosely on DNS resolvers and servers. A Map-Server publishes the mappings that routers register with it, and a Map-Resolver answers lookups from routers without requiring those routers to participate in the complex database infrastructure.
sections.eli5: LISP needs to know where everyone is on the Internet. Instead of making every router learn the whole database, there is a front desk (Map-Server and Map-Resolver) that keeps track of the information and answers questions.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
Map-Server: A network device that learns mappings from routers and publishes them to the mapping database on their behalf. Map-Resolver: A network device that routers query to look up where an EID is located. It consults the mapping database and returns the answer.

Encapsulated Map-Request: A special query message sent to UDP port 4342 that is wrapped in an extra LISP header. Map-Register: A message sent by a router to a Map-Server to register the prefixes it serves. Map-Notify: A confirmation message sent back by the Map-Server when it receives a Map-Register.

Negative Map-Reply: A response indicating that the requested address is not in the LISP system, sent with an action code of "Natively-Forward" to tell the querying router to use normal Internet routing.
sections.eli5: A Map-Server remembers where things are. A Map-Resolver looks things up. A Map-Register says "I am here now". A Negative Map-Reply says "I do not know where that is."

sections.title: How the Mapping Service Works
sections.content:
An Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) that needs to send traffic to an Endpoint ID first queries a configured Map-Resolver with an Encapsulated Map-Request. The Map-Resolver looks up the EID in the mapping database system and returns a Map-Reply with the RLOC of the router serving that EID. If the EID is not in the system, it returns a Negative Map-Reply.

On the registration side, an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) periodically sends Map-Register messages to a configured Map-Server to announce the Endpoint ID prefixes it serves. The Map-Server stores these mappings and publishes them to the database. The ETR can request proxy reply service by setting the P-bit (proxy bit), in which case the Map-Server answers queries on its behalf instead of forwarding them.

The Map-Resolver and Map-Server can be the same device. This design lets routers avoid implementing the database protocols (like LISP+ALT, which uses BGP and GRE tunnels) themselves.
sections.eli5: A router asks the desk "where is this address?" The desk looks it up and says "ask this person." Or the desk can say "I know the answer: they are here."

sections.title: Registration and Resolution
sections.content:
Map-Register messages are sent at least once per minute, with a suggested interval of one minute. The Map-Server should remove a registration if it does not receive a refresh within three minutes. An ETR may increase the frequency to once every 20 seconds in the first five minutes after startup (the "quick registration" period).

The ETR can set the M-bit (want-map-notify) in a Map-Register to request confirmation. The Map-Server responds with a Map-Notify message to UDP port 4342. If the ETR requests proxy reply service (P-bit), it must include all the RLOCs of all ETRs serving that prefix, along with flags indicating which RLOCs are routable.

When a Map-Resolver receives an Encapsulated Map-Request, it first checks if it has the mapping in a local cache. If it knows the mapping, it returns a Map-Reply. If it knows the EID does not exist, it returns a Negative Map-Reply with a 15-minute Time to Live. If it needs more information, it forwards the request to the mapping database.
sections.eli5: Every minute, a router tells the desk "I serve this address, find me here." The desk remembers for three minutes. When another router asks the desk "where is that?" the desk either answers or forwards the question to someone who knows.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
To prevent EID-prefix hijacking, a Map-Server must be configured with the exact EID-Prefixes that each ETR is authorized to register. It rejects any Map-Register claiming a prefix that is not in the configuration.

Map-Register messages include authentication data: a hash computed using a pair-wise shared key between the ETR and Map-Server. The RFC requires support for HMAC-SHA-1-96 and recommends HMAC-SHA-256-128. Keys are configured manually during experimental deployment.

The 2-way LISP header nonce exchange (documented in RFC 6830) can be used to prevent spoofing attacks. The RFC notes that the current authentication mechanism does not protect against replay attacks, and refers to LISP-SEC (an extension specification) for proposed solutions including anti-replay protection and prevention of overclaiming attacks.
sections.eli5: Only routers with the right secret key can register. When a router registers, it proves it knows the secret. But someone could play back an old message, so better security is being worked on.
